reference_answers: The Occupy LA encampment got a stay of execution this morning—though a few arrests have been reported beyond the boundaries of City Hall Park. Two hours after protesters defied city hall's order to vacate the park by 12:01am, lawyer and Occupy supporter Jim Lafferty told Reuters he expected police to give the camp a two-day reprieve. At around 5am, police told protesters over a loudspeaker that they didn't intend to clear the park, the LA Times reports. Police do, however, intend to clear protesters out of the street, and several people who refused to move out of an intersection have already been arrested. "We definitely need to get morning traffic in," a police commander explained. Everything also seems calm at Occupy Philadelphia, where protesters defied a 5pm Sunday deadline to disperse. But as of last night, a police inspector said they didn't intend to forcibly evict anyone. "We look forward to working with Occupy Philadelphia and a resolution of the problem," he told the Philadelphia Inquirer. "Confrontation is never good."

Occupy Philadelphia remained on site at City Hall into the evening of November 28, despite Mayor Nutter's deadline for them to vacate the area. The protesters had been given a 5 p.m. Sunday deadline to leave, but did not comply until late in the evening. The police did not enforce the eviction, and Mayor Nutter stated that he did not want to use force against the protesters. The Occupy Philadelphia movement has been relatively peaceful and cooperative, with protesters chanting slogans such as "What does democracy look like? This is what democracy looks like." The protesters have been met with police presence, but have not been forcibly removed.

In other cities, such as Philadelphia, protesters have been met with more force. In Philadelphia, the Occupy Philadelphia movement has been allowed to remain on site, but other cities such as Oakland have seen more violent confrontations between protesters and police. In Los Angeles, Mayor Villaraigosa had given the Occupy LA protesters until midnight to vacate the City Hall park, but later allowed them to stay until daybreak.

The Occupy movement has gained momentum and support from various groups, including labor unions and clergy, as they continue to protest economic inequality and the excesses of the U.S. financial system. The movement has also been met with resistance from some city officials, who have attempted to evict the protesters and have criticized the movement for causing disruptions and posing a safety hazard.

Overall, the Occupy movement has brought attention to the growing income inequality in the United States and has sparked a national conversation about the role of corporations and the government in addressing these issues. While the movement has faced challenges and resistance, it has also gained support and has the potential to continue to bring about change.

reference_answers: Fixer Upper stars Chip and Joanna Gaines are having to pay up for EPA violations seen on their hit HGTV show. The couple's business, Magnolia Homes, has agreed to pay a $40,000 fine after the EPA determined 33 of its home renovations were "conducted without adequate lead paint protections," reports Deadline, which notes the potential fine the company faced was as high as $556,000. The EPA notes Fixer Upper footage "reviewed by EPA did not depict the lead-safe work practices normally required" though "Magnolia took immediate steps to ensure compliance" when it was notified. Chip Gaines, who in March tweeted advice about engaging a professional to check for lead paint when buying or remodeling a home, will also star in a Magnolia-paid video on lead paint safety as part of the settlement, per Vulture. (The couple are expecting their fifth child.)
samples.text: Magnolia Homes, the renovation firm featured on the HGTV show Fixer Upper, has agreed to pay a $40,000 civil penalty to the EPA for alleged violations of the Toxic Substances Control Act's Lead Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule. The company was found to have not taken adequate precautions while renovating homes that contained lead paint, as depicted on the show. Magnolia and its co-owner Chip Gaines have also agreed to produce and release an educational video highlighting the dangers of lead-based paint within 90 days, and spend $160,000 on a lead-abatement project in their hometown of Waco, Texas. The settlement requires Magnolia to take steps to ensure compliance with lead-based paint regulations in future renovations and to improve the public's appreciation for the serious hazards of lead-based paint contained in older homes and the precautions necessary to reduce those hazards.

reference_answers: Another fatality in the Boston bombings has been identified: The family of 29-year-old Krystle Campbell says she was killed as she and a friend were cheering on another friend who was racing, reports WCVB. "This is just a waste," says her mother. “Everyone that knew her loved her. She was always smiling. You couldn’t ask for a better daughter. She was the best.” Campbell was a restaurant manager, reports the Boston Herald, which notes an especially wrenching detail: Her father was initially told she was alive, but when he got to the ICU, he realized it was his daughter's friend who had survived. Campbell is the second of the three people killed to be identified. The first was 8-year-old Martin Richard, and his father, Bill, released a statement today thanking supporters and asking for privacy, reports WBZ. "My dear son Martin has died from injuries sustained in the attack on Boston. My wife and daughter are both recovering from serious injuries. We thank our family and friends, those we know and those we have never met, for their thoughts and prayers. I ask that you continue to pray for my family as we remember Martin. We also ask for your patience and for privacy as we work to simultaneously grieve and recover. Thank you." The third victim was a grad student at Boston University, but the person's identity is being withheld until the family says it's OK to release, reports USA Today.

The Boston Marathon bombings on April 15, 2013, resulted in the deaths of three people and injured more than 260 others. The victims included 8-year-old Martin Richard, 29-year-old Krystle Campbell, and a third victim whose identity was withheld pending family permission. The two bombs exploded near the finish line of the marathon, causing chaos and destruction.

The first victim identified was 8-year-old Martin Richard, who was at the marathon to watch his father, a community leader in Dorchester, run. His mother, Denise, and sister, 9-year-old Sarah, were both injured in the blasts. Martin's father, Bill Richard, released a statement expressing his gratitude for the outpouring of support from the community and the world.

Krystle Campbell, a restaurant manager from Medford, Massachusetts, was the second victim to be identified. She was waiting near the finish line to cheer on a friend who was running when she was killed.

The third victim was identified as a Chinese graduate student who was watching the marathon with two friends. The Chinese Consulate in New York confirmed the student's death, and the university did not release the student's name or gender, pending family approval.

The city of Boston was grappling with the process of identifying its dead, a strong police presence on its streets, and a firm resolve to heal and move forward. The mayor promised that the city would not be intimidated by terror, and the police promised to go to the ends of the Earth to find whoever was responsible.

The Salvation Army mobilized four mobile kitchens and more than 30 people to provide food, drinks, and emotional and spiritual care. The First Corps of Cadets Armory in downtown Boston, unofficially known as "The Castle," became a staging area for runners looking for their gear bags, trying to find lost phones and passports or trying to make travel arrangements.

The blasts occurred just hours after Ethiopia's Lelisa Desisa won the 26.2-mile race. The race was stopped, and the marathon headquarters were locked down. The Federal Aviation Administration announced a temporary flight restriction over Boston.

The tragedy brought words of encouragement and solidarity from across the nation and around the world. President Obama praised first responders and others who helped the injured. The Pope also sent word to Cardinal Sean O'Malley, archbishop of Boston, that he was "deeply grieved" by the bombings. The Pope prayed that all would be "united in a resolve not to be overcome by evil, but to combat evil with good, working together to build an ever more just, free and secure society for generations yet to come."

In the aftermath of the bombings, the city of Boston and its residents showed strength, compassion, and determination to see justice done. The community came together to support the victims and their families, and the city continued to heal and move forward.
